transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-10-22
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 75 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Elena Morris (Redwood SE), Priya Reddy (CTO, Nimbus), Marcus Lee (ML Infra), Aisha Khan (Security)

Summary (auto): Workshop to align on benchmark methodology and on-prem pilot scope.

[00:00] Samir: hey everyone, thanks for making time. quick agenda - apples to apples bench methodology, prompt sets we should use, load generation and tooling, and then a walkthrough for on-prem / VPC constraints. Elena will lead the runtime deep dive.
[00:28] Priya: thanks, Samir. our main ask is: we want a clean comparison between our current infra and what Redwood offers, but we also need to prove it inside our VPC. security is a hard stop for any data leaving our network.
[00:45] Elena: totally understood. we'll cover both hosted and on-prem runs. first question - what are your representative prompt sets? are these chat-style multi-turn, single-turn completions, or lots of short queries like embeddings?
[01:10] Marcus: primarily multi-turn chat for customer support workflows, and a smaller bulk of high-rate short prompts for monitoring/alerts. average context is around 512 tokens, with tail up to 2k for a few flows.
[01:35] Elena: ok that matters a lot, because KV cache hit rates and sequence length distribution change the effective throughput. if you have long tails, quantization choices can amplify latency for cold starts.
[02:05] Aisha: on the security side, we need to see KMS integration, and any logs that leave the VPC must be sanitized. also SOC 2 requirements - retention windows and audit logs.
[02:28] Samir: we'll share our security pack - SOC2 2024 report, KMS patterns for private deployments, and recommended audit settings. note that on some on-prem installs we can use customer-managed HSM.
[02:50] Priya: great. on apples-to-apples, we want to match model versions, tokenization, and batching configs. also, we need to understand how you measure latency: p95, p99, and tail behaviors under load.
[03:18] Elena: our recommended baseline is p50/p90/p99 across synthetic load that mirrors your request arrival distribution. we also measure cold-start impact and the effect of KV cache warm-up. we usually run steady-state for 15 minutes and capture tok/s and GPU utilization.
[03:48] Marcus: what tooling do you use for load generation? we have terraform-coded infra for our load agents.
[04:05] Elena: we use a harness built on locust for per-request modeling and a k6 script for higher throughput, plus a smaller Go-based client that hits the streaming endpoint. I'll share the harness repo (link) after the call.
[04:25] Samir: note: the repo includes configs for sequence length distributions, variable concurrency, and KV-cache warm-up scenarios.
[04:40] [link] Redwood benchmark harness: https://github.com/redwood-inference/benchmarks (private)
[05:00] Priya: perfect. about quantization - our infra team saw big delta with 4-bit quant on some models; accuracy regressed slightly. how do you recommend validating quality regressions?
[05:25] Elena: you want a small evaluation prompt-set and automated BLEU/ROUGE-like plus embedding-similarity checks; we also run a small human eval on a sample. quantization configs should be kept consistent between runs - e.g., GPT-style fp16 baseline vs q4_0. avoid mixing per-layer quant schemes unless you annotate them.
[06:00] Marcus: and batching? we care about latency SLOs - if we increase batch size for throughput does the p99 blow up?
[06:20] Elena: it depends on request arrival distribution. continuous batching helps maintain throughput with small latency impact for many workloads, but for strict p99 SLO you need smaller max batch cap and prefer KV caching. We recommend testing several batch caps (e.g., 1, 8, 32) and observing p50/p99. The harness supports that sweep.
[06:50] Priya: about KV cache - can you explain warm-up heuristics? we have a lot of repeated prefixes for the chat flow.
[07:05] Elena: KV cache keeps key/value states per session; warm-up is twofold: synthetic warm-up where you replay common prefixes, and live-warm-up where the model accumulates KV entries. We also have eviction policies based on session LRU and max cache size. For benchmarking, you should run a warm-up phase (10-20% of test length) to reach steady-state hit-rate.
[07:40] Samir: also add a cold-start run to capture first-request tail. Many customers want both numbers.
[07:50] [08:30] Marcus: for on-prem pilots, network matters - TLS termination, egress rules, and peering. our security team requires strict egress and no external control-plane traffic that contains PII. how have you done VPC/onprem in other customers?
[08:55] Elena: we offer a private control plane option where all inference traffic stays in your VPC; telemetry can be pushed to an S3 bucket or a local SIEM. For fully air-gapped setups we ship a bundle and pair via an offline license; in that case you manage KMS locally. runs are performed by our runtime service inside customer's infra.
[09:25] Aisha: do you require any outgoing connections to Redwood for model updates?
[09:35] Samir: model updates are optional; you can opt to pull updates via an internal mirror or have Redwood push updates if network rules allow. For the pilot we'll recommend a mirror approach to satisfy compliance.
[09:50] Elena: back to bench details - apples-to-apples means we fix: model weights, tokenizer, sequence length cap, batch cap, quantization mode, KV cache enabled/disabled, and measurement windows. If Nimbus can provide the exact tokenization script you use, we can incorporate it to avoid subtle differences.
[10:20] Priya: yes, we'll export our tokenizer and send over. Marcus will also provide histograms of seq lengths.
[10:35] Marcus: note: some of our logs are noisy; I'll sanitize before sharing.
[10:45] Samir: good. let's talk about metrics: we'll report p50/p90/p99 latency, tokens-per-second, GPU utilization, and cost-per-1M tokens estimate for hosted and per-hour GPU cost for on-prem.
[11:10] Priya: cost estimates are important. we also want to see how autoscaling affects tail latencies under bursty traffic.
[11:25] Elena: we can simulate burst patterns in the harness - e.g., 10x spike for 60s every 10 minutes. For autoscaling we run separate experiments: fixed capacity, autoscale with cold-start penalties, and overprovisioned baseline.
[11:50] Marcus: question on measuring KV cache effect: do you recommend per-session keys or a shared cache?
[12:05] Elena: per-session gives best semantic correctness and avoids cross-user leakage; shared caches can help for highly similar public queries but are tricky for privacy. For benchmarking, run both: session-local and global with controlled prefixes.
[12:35] Aisha: privacy concern - if shared cache is used, we need guarantees about keys and masking. can you include a mode that strips user identifiers before caching?
[12:50] Elena: yes we have pre-processing hooks. we can instrument the harness to run a scrub step on request before caching. we'll document it.
[13:10] Priya: on quantization again - you mentioned accuracy checks; what thresholds do you recommend for acceptable regression?
[13:25] Elena: typically <2% delta on your primary metric (e.g., answer correctness / embedding cosine distance) is considered acceptable for many workloads; frank discussion needed for high-stakes domains. we log per-prompt delta so you can decide which prompts degrade.
[13:50] Samir: we'll produce a template quality report that shows delta per-prompt and aggregated.
[14:05] [14:40] Marcus: practical question - what GPU stack are you expecting for the on-prem pilot? we have A10G and a couple of A100s; budget for more is limited.
[14:55] Elena: that's helpful. A100 performs better at fp16, but quantization gives good perf on A10G too. We'll configure kernel choices in the runtime to match architecture. For apples-to-apples, we'll report normalized tokens-per-second per GPU and give absolute latency numbers.
[15:20] Priya: network egress - if we do a private control plane, how do we handle telemetry?
[15:35] Elena: telemetry can be pushed to an S3-compatible store in your VPC or to a local Elastic cluster; logs that leave the VPC can be routed to your SIEM via a pull model. We'll provide config examples.
[15:55] Aisha: if telemetry contains request text, that could be a PII vector. we need filters.
[16:10] Elena: agreed - we'll show how to mask or redact at ingestion and what fields are safe to export.
[16:30] Samir: let's outline the pilot plan: 1) exchange prompts and tokenizer, 2) Redwood sends benchmark harness + example configs, 3) Nimbus provices infra diagram + peering rules, 4) run a smoke test in your VPC, 5) run full apples-to-apples suite with warm-up and cold-start runs, 6) produce report.
[17:00] Priya: timeline looks good. can we do the smoke test next week?
[17:10] Samir: target next week - Elena and Marcus to pick a slot. I'll follow up via email.
[17:20] [17:50] Marcus: one more detail on load - do you measure tokenization time as part of the latency bucket? we pre-tokenize on client side for some flows.
[18:05] Elena: good point. we capture end-to-end including tokenization for client-side measurement, but we also break out server-side inference time. For apples-to-apples, specify whether you pre-tokenize; otherwise tokenization differences can skew latency.
[18:30] Priya: we'll standardize on server-side tokenization for the benchmark to keep things simple.
[18:45] Samir: got it. Also we'll provide a config sheet with fields: model, tokenizer, seq cap, batch cap, quant mode, kv cache (on/off), warm-up length, measurement window, burst pattern.
[19:05] Elena: and we'll include GPU metrics collection - nvidia-smi logs, DCGM, and process-level mem usage.
[19:25] Marcus: please include a small script to parse DCGM csv into graphs.
[19:40] Elena: done, in the harness.
[19:50] [20:30] Aisha: compliance question - for audit logs we need immutable timestamps and retention policy. can Redwood support S3 object lock or equivalent?
[20:45] Samir: yes for the private deployments we can integrate with S3 object lock or a customer-managed retention policy. We'll include options in the security pack.
[21:05] Priya: are there known regressions for certain quantization modes with long-context models? we saw in-house issues with q2_* in some tests.
[21:25] Elena: q2 can give big memory gains but often hurts quality on long-context generative tasks - q4 variants are generally safer. We'll show per-prompt deltas.
[21:50] Marcus: for our apples-to-apples comparison, do you have a suggested control baseline? like HF fp16 with X kernels?
[22:10] Elena: recommended baseline: fp16 with vendor-optimized kernels (e.g., cuBLAS/flash attention enabled) + same tokenizer. If you're using another vendor runtime, include its config so we can reproduce.
[22:35] Samir: also include version pins for libs (torch/transformers/runtime). small version diffs can change perf.
[22:50] Priya: okay we'll capture environment details.
[23:05] [23:40] Elena: one more runtime note - continuous batching logic and KV cache interplay can reduce the number of forward passes per token by up to 40% in some chat workloads. That improves tokens-per-second but can slightly shift latency distribution. We'll show trade-offs in the report.
[24:05] Marcus: useful. can you show an example of config that favors latency SLO vs throughput?
[24:20] Elena: example: latency SLO config - batch_cap=8, max_concurrency=32, kv_cache_enabled=true, quant=q4_0; throughput config - batch_cap=64, max_concurrency=256, aggressive continuous batching, possibly q4_1. we'll annotate expected tradeoffs.
[24:50] Priya: for the on-prem pilot, what telemetry ports do you need open? we are strict on port allowances.
[25:05] Elena: minimal ports: HTTPS control plane port (optional), gRPC/HTTP endpoints for inference inside VPC, and metrics export port for Prometheus if you want scrape-based telemetry. We'll send exact port list.
[25:30] Samir: note that if using private control plane, control-plane ports can be locked to specific IPs.
[25:45] [26:20] Marcus: recording notes - we'll need to run baseline + 3 experiments: 1) fp16 baseline, 2) q4_0, 3) q4_1 plus batch sweep.
[26:35] Elena: agreed. also add cold-start and warm-up runs plus a burst pattern.
[26:50] Aisha: for the audit trail, please add a checksum for the harness artifacts we exchange.
[27:05] Samir: will do.
[27:30] Priya: any red flags we should watch for during pilot?
[27:45] Elena: watch KV cache eviction and memory pressure - on smaller GPUs aggressive batching can cause OOM. We'll provide instance sizing guidance. Also watch network egress latency for control-plane calls.
[28:05] Marcus: we'll schedule resource headroom for the pilot.
[28:20] [28:55] Samir: last administrative - I'll share a calendar invite for the smoke test and attach the harness link.
[29:10] Priya: thanks, looking forward.
[29:20] Elena: thanks everyone.

(Transcription ends - remaining discussion was scheduling and logistics, captured in action items.)
